lessons.objectiveEnglish: Say breakfast words clearly and greet a server or barista politely in the morning.
lessons.focusFrench: Salutations avec vous ; les sons é/è, u/ou et eu/œu, les voyelles nasales, le r et les lettres finales muettes.

words.noteEnglish: Pronounced kah-FAY, stress on the last syllable. Alone, un café in France usually means an espresso.
Pronounced ZHÜ (the French j is like the s in 'measure'). Orange juice is le jus d'orange.
Pronounced LEH; the final t is silent.
Borrowed from Spanish and used in French for the Mexican flatbread; pronounced tor-TEE-ya.
Borrowed word, pronounced approximately TCHOO-ro with a French r; unlike the usual French ch sound.
Pronounced leh-ZUH in the plural (liaison of the s). Singular un œuf is pronounced uhf.
Pronounced SÜ-kr; the final e is silent and the r is soft.
In a café, la carte lists what you can order; un menu is usually a set-price meal.
Pain has a nasal vowel [pɛ̃]; do not pronounce the final n.
Use from morning until early evening; then say Bonsoir.
Vous is the polite form for a server or someone you do not know.

words.en: My name is Sam, nice to meet you.
words.noteEnglish: Say enchantée if the speaker is a woman.

words.en: Thank you very much, see you tomorrow!

words.noteEnglish: Standard polite goodbye in shops and cafés; bonne journée works with anyone.

lessons.speakingFrench: Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Sam, enchanté. Un café, un jus, du lait et des œufs, s'il vous plaît.

english: Sam greets the barista Rosa in Oaxaca: Good morning!
Rosa: Hi, how are you?
Sam: My name is Sam, nice to meet you.
Sam reads the menu and orders an orange juice.
Sam also orders a coffee with milk.
Sam doesn't put sugar in the coffee.
To eat, Sam orders eggs with tortillas.
Rosa recommends a churro and sweet bread.
Sam: Thank you very much, see you tomorrow!
french: Sam salue la barista Rosa à Oaxaca : Bonjour !
Rosa : Bonjour, comment allez-vous ?
Sam : Je m'appelle Sam, enchanté.
Sam lit la carte et commande un jus d'orange.
Sam commande aussi un café au lait.
Sam ne met pas de sucre dans le café.
Pour manger, Sam commande des œufs avec des tortillas.
Rosa recommande un churro et du pain sucré.
Sam : Merci beaucoup, à demain !

teachingNotesEnglish: In the Oaxaca scene, a churro and tortillas are named foods; pain sucré means sweet bread. A French café often sells pastries called viennoiseries.
FRANCE USAGE: Bonjour is used from morning until early evening; Bonsoir follows. In Québec, Belgium and Switzerland, breakfast is often le déjeuner rather than le petit-déjeuner.
Use vous with a server or stranger. Enchanté changes to enchantée when the speaker is a woman.
FRANCE USAGE: un café alone commonly means espresso; un café au lait is usually a breakfast drink. At a café, un crème is a common coffee-with-milk order.
French ch is usually sh (chat); j is the zh of measure; French r is made in the back of the throat, not rolled.

French writing has six vowel letters (a, e, i, o, u, y) and many vowel sounds: é/è, u/ou, eu/œu and nasal vowels (pain, bonjour). The accents in é and è show vowel quality; other accents can distinguish words in writing.
lessons.objectiveFrenchCourseEnglish: Greet a café server politely and pronounce common breakfast words clearly in French.
lessons.speakingInstructionEnglish: Greet the barista with Bonjour, say your name, and pronounce café, jus, lait and œufs clearly.
lessons.focusEnglish: Polite morning greetings with vous; French é/è, u/ou and eu/œu, nasal vowels, the French r, and silent final letters.

lessons.objectiveEnglish: Use numbers, prices in pesos, clock times and café quantities to order and check a total.
lessons.focusFrench: Nombres 0–1 000 : vingt et un, soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix, cent/deux cents, mille ; heures et demie ; prix à la tasse et à la pièce.

words.noteEnglish: Pesos are the currency in this Mexico scene; in French, pronounce pay-ZOH with a silent final s.
Pronounced 'leur'. Quelle heure est-il ? means what time is it?
Pronounced luh mah-TAN.
Pronounced mee-DEE. Le midi on its own means lunchtime.
Pronounced 'tahss'.
Le verre is a glass. For a takeaway cup, say un gobelet; à emporter means to take away.
Use la pièce for a unit price: 20 pesos la pièce. Count pastries directly when ordering.
Pronounced por-SYON. One plate of chilaquiles is one portion.
Pronounced doo-ZEN.
For a slice of cake: une part de gâteau. Pronounced 'par'.
In France, un allongé is common for espresso diluted with hot water; café américain is intelligible but can also mean filter coffee.

words.fr: Une table pour 4, s'il vous plaît.

words.noteEnglish: Natural order in French; pain sucré means sweet bread. A French café may instead sell viennoiseries.
Ça fait... ? is the everyday French for 'That comes to...?'

words.fr: Il est huit heures et demie.
words.noteEnglish: Written form: Il est 8 h 30.

words.fr: Le petit-déjeuner, c'est de 7 h à 11 h ?

lessons.speakingFrench: Deux cafés et trois pains sucrés, s'il vous plaît. Ça fait cent vingt pesos ?

english: Emma walks into Café Luna in the morning.
Emma looks at the time: It's half past 8.
Luis: There are servings of chilaquiles until noon.
Emma: 2 americanos, please.
Luis: The cup costs 30 pesos and the glass 35.
Emma: In a cup, and 3 pieces of sweet bread.
Luis: The piece costs 20 pesos and the dozen 200.
Emma: Is it 120 pesos?
Luis: Yes, and the slice of cake costs 45.
french: Un matin, Emma entre au Café Luna.
Emma regarde l'heure : Il est huit heures et demie.
Luis : On sert des portions de chilaquiles jusqu'à midi.
Emma : 2 cafés américains, s'il vous plaît.
Luis : C'est 30 pesos la tasse et 35 le verre.
Emma : En tasse, et 3 pains sucrés.
Luis : C'est 20 pesos la pièce et 200 la douzaine.
Emma : Ça fait 120 pesos ?
Luis : Oui, et la part de gâteau coûte 45.

teachingNotesEnglish: This Mexico café scene uses pesos, chilaquiles and Café Luna. A café elsewhere may use a different currency.
Pain sucré means sweet bread. In France, a bakery or café may offer a viennoiserie instead.
FRANCE USAGE: Ça fait combien ? asks the total. A slice of cake is une part de gâteau; la pièce can state a unit price.
FRANCE USAGE: un allongé is a common café order; café américain is intelligible but can also refer to filter coffee.

NUMBERS: 21 = vingt et un, 70 = soixante-dix, 80 = quatre-vingts, 90 = quatre-vingt-dix, 100 = cent, 120 = cent vingt, 200 = deux cents, 220 = deux cent vingt, 1 000 = mille. Cent takes s only when multiplied and final; quatre-vingts loses s when another number follows. In standard France usage, 81 = quatre-vingt-un and 91 = quatre-vingt-onze (no et); Belgium and Switzerland also use septante/nonante, and some Swiss cantons use huitante.
TIME: Il est huit heures et demie, but midi et demi. Timetables often use 24-hour notation: 15 h = 3 pm; 8 h 30 = 8:30.
lessons.objectiveFrenchCourseEnglish: Use French numbers, clock times and café quantities to order and check a total in this Mexico travel scene.
lessons.speakingInstructionEnglish: Order two coffees and three pieces of sweet bread from a barista, then repeat the total in pesos to check it.
lessons.focusEnglish: French numbers to 1,000, including 70/80/90; café prices by cup or piece; clock times and quantities.

lessons.objectiveEnglish: Describe food, drinks and tables at a café with ser and estar.
lessons.focusFrench: Être + adjectif pour les choses (le café est chaud) ; accord masculin/féminin et singulier/pluriel ; questions polies avec l'intonation ou est-ce que. Pour une personne : j'ai chaud/froid, jamais je suis chaud.

words.noteEnglish: Feminine: chaude. Pronounced SHOH.
Feminine: froide, as in la boisson est froide. For how you feel, say j'ai froid.
Feminine: fraîche. Le pain est frais.
Sucré is the safe word for sweet to taste. Doux means mild or soft, but can mean sweet for wine or cider.
Feminine: piquante. Épicé means spiced, not necessarily hot; for chili heat say piquant or ça pique.
Feminine: délicieuse.
Feminine: occupée.
The same form for both genders: libre.
Masculine: le serveur. Pronounced sair-VUHZ.
French uses être for both the temporary state and the lasting quality. Très means very.
Natural spoken question with rising intonation. Est-ce que cette table est libre ? is another neutral option; inversion is more formal.
Du jour means made today in café usage. For origin, say le café vient du Mexique.
Salsa is Mexican here; the feminine agreement is piquante.
A man says prêt; a woman says je suis prête.

lessons.speakingFrench: Cette table est libre ? Mon café est chaud et la salsa est très piquante.

english: Daniel is at a café in Oaxaca, and many tables are taken.
Daniel asks the server: Is this table free?
The server, Rosa, says: Yes, it is free.
Daniel: Is the bread from today?
Rosa: Yes, the sweet bread is fresh.
Daniel: I'm ready to order.
Rosa brings coffee, orange juice and chilaquiles with salsa.
Daniel: The coffee is very hot, but the juice is cold.
Daniel: The salsa is very spicy, but it is delicious.
french: Daniel est dans un café à Oaxaca, et beaucoup de tables sont occupées.
Daniel demande à la serveuse : Cette table est libre ?
La serveuse, Rosa, dit : Oui, elle est libre.
Daniel : Le pain est du jour ?
Rosa : Oui, le pain sucré est frais.
Daniel : Je suis prêt à commander.
Rosa apporte du café, du jus d'orange et des chilaquiles avec de la salsa.
Daniel : Le café est très chaud, mais le jus est froid.
Daniel : La salsa est très piquante, mais elle est délicieuse.

teachingNotesEnglish: French uses être to describe food and tables, with adjective agreement; it does not have the Spanish ser/estar distinction.
Être describes objects here. A person says j'ai chaud or j'ai froid, never je suis chaud to mean temperature.
Adjective agreement: chaud/chaude, froid/froide, frais/fraîche, occupé/occupée. Plural adds -s: occupé, occupés, occupée, occupées (les tables sont occupées).
This Oaxaca café serves salsa and chilaquiles. Pain sucré means sweet bread in French.
You can ask a café question with rising intonation or est-ce que. Fixed phrases like comment allez-vous are useful now; productive inversion comes later.
FRANCE USAGE: petit-déjeuner is breakfast; in Québec, Belgium and Switzerland le déjeuner can mean breakfast.
lessons.titleFrenchCourseEnglish: Describing Food and Tables with Être
lessons.objectiveFrenchCourseEnglish: Describe food, drinks and available tables in French with être and adjective agreement.
lessons.speakingInstructionEnglish: Ask a server if a table is free, then describe whether your coffee is hot or cold and whether the salsa is spicy.
lessons.focusEnglish: Describe objects with être and adjective agreement; ask natural café questions with intonation or est-ce que. For how a person feels, say j'ai chaud or j'ai froid.
